items.title: Toward a Politics of Planetary Care: The Limits of More‐Than‐Human Approaches, Silenced Notes From Indigenous Forest Worlds in India
items.affiliation: Museum of the History of Science

extra.summary: ABSTRACT In response to the planetary climate crisis, influential scholarship has directed us to decenter the human, recognize nonhuman agency, and imagine more‐than‐human futures. But what might this leave out? Drawing on Indigenous forest worlds in India and the incarcerated intellectual‐activists who struggled alongside them, this article develops a politics of planetary care. Planetary care begins from the proposition that all life is interdependent, but that life is being sustained under profoundly unequal conditions. Bringing Indigenous forest worlds into conversation with feminist theories of care and social reproduction, the article asks how the conditions that make life possible are sustained, by whom, and how capitalist extraction, state violence, and conjugated social oppression determine whose lives, labor, and environments are valued—and whose are rendered expendable. Care, it argues, is not simply an ethical disposition or a practice of lifemaking but a political struggle to defend and transform the conditions through which human and more‐than‐human life is sustained. In doing so, the article asks which Indigenous ideas are allowed to travel as planetary theory and which remain conceptually incarcerated within the domains of ontology, cosmology, and more‐than‐human relationality.

items.title: Fugitive Anthropology: Embodying Activist Research

extra.summary: Estradathe volume expands on provocations leveled in their "Toward a Fugitive Anthropology" published in Cultural Anthropology (Berry et al. 2017 ).Fifteen mostly ethnographic, often deeply personal essays by an intergenerational, international set of authors thoroughly demonstrate how the ethnographer's body matters in the field, as both subject to power and constitutive of liberatory knowledges.From this foundational claim, they argue for the importance of cultivating deeper solidarities and fuller forms of accountability with collaborators.

items.title: Toward an Indigenous Curatorial Practice: Learning From Tłıchǫ Metaphors of Care to Establish Principles of Curation

extra.summary: ABSTRACT The displacement of items of cultural heritage from Indigenous communities is continually perpetuated through their appropriation into collection systems that are inappropriate to Indigenous laws and customs. This paper presents the efforts of the Tłı̨chǫ Government (TG) to address such issues by creating a system that is rooted within its values and traditions for the curation of its cultural heritage. It is embarking on this journey through the creation of its digital archive and the development of programming for its community museum in Behchokǫ̀, Northwest Territories (NWT), Canada. This process first entailed stepping back to carefully consider Tłı̨chǫ traditions of caring for knowledge and cultural heritage through learning circles and a Strong like Two methodology. Analyses of these results were then used to infer principles of curation—ownership, preservation, stewardship, and categorization. This research contributes to the decolonization of the field of cultural heritage management (CHM) and presents a leading example of how the exercise of sovereignty over cultural heritage by Indigenous Nations stands to reactivate displaced belongings within their communities.

items.title: Spectral Ecologies: Sintering More‐Than‐Human Pasts to Less‐Than‐Certain Futures

extra.summary: ABSTRACT How do we mourn the loss of more‐than‐human beings, and what becomes of them when they are gone? This commentary examines two installations in Spectral Remix , an art exhibition at the 2025 American Anthropological Association Annual Meeting in New Orleans. The first is Cymene Howe and Dominic Boyer's Glacier Graveyard , which memorializes glaciers lost to anthropogenic climate change. The second is the XYZ Collective's The Atlas of Heritage Trees , which uses laser scanning, 3D printing, and digital animation to rematerialize ancient trees now threatened by climate change and saltwater intrusion. Drawing on embodied and affective encounters with each installation, I show how Glacier Graveyard extends human funerary rituals to glaciers through an immersive and visceral encounter, while The Atlas of Heritage Trees imagines uncanny technoscientific afterlives for dying trees as they are translated into digital forms. I engage the analytic of sintering —which refers to both the physical process that bonds ephemeral snowflakes into durable glacial ice and an advanced laser technique used in 3D printing—to examine uncanny resonances across these two more‐than‐human works. Taken together, these works show how installation as a medium can facilitate a deeper reckoning with more‐than‐human pasts and less‐than‐certain futures, forcing us to confront which bonds we choose to make and which bonds we choose to break in our shared worlds.

items.title: Becoming climate sentinels
items.affiliation: Victoria University of Wellington; Victoria University

extra.summary: Abstract In South Korea, forest scientists refashion themselves as “climate sentinels” as they confront subtle yet disquieting shifts in plant seasonality brought about by climate change. Unlike traditional sentinels, who watch for external threats from a frontier, climate sentinels face ecological anomalies and surprises—such as untimely flowering—that have permeated everyday spaces. To register such ecological perplexities, they engage in technoscientific entrainments: deliberate, disciplinary, and laborious coordinations of human observers, trees, protocols, institutions, and modular devices into a shared rhythm of attention. These experimental processes redistribute the traditional embodied technique of mokch’ŭk (eye observation) across nationwide phenological observation networks while reanimating the ecological significance of plant seasonality. For these sentinels, confronting climate change requires attending not only to satellites and heavily computed models but also to the distributed, more‐than‐human experiments through which ecological perplexities are made sensible on the ground.

items.title: Reassessment of the morphological evidence for hominin hybrids in the Levant
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute
items.affiliation: University College London; University of Reading; Natural History Museum

extra.summary: The Levantine hominin fossil and archaeological records have played a central role in long‐standing palaeoanthropological debates over origin models and possible interbreeding between Neanderthals ( Homo neanderthalensis ) and Homo sapiens . Recent research has provided a strong framework for the morphological expectations of recent hybrid ancestry in primates, along with renewed suggestions that early Late Pleistocene hominins from the Levant show morphological evidence of hybridization. Here we address these developments by using established diagnostic features of H. sapiens and H. neanderthalensis to review possible fossil evidence of hybridization from the key Levantine sites of Qafzeh, Skhūl, and Tabūn. We conclude that, while individuals from these sites show a perplexing combination of characteristics that broadly overlap with expectations of hybridization, this explanation can only be established once other alternatives have been ruled out, or through the recovery of genetic material from these key fossils.

items.title: On Friendship’s Mystic Affordances (Also, On Universalism, Particularism, and the Generic)
items.source: Comparative Studies in Society and History

extra.summary: Abstract Four recent monographs have inspired me to reflect on studying friendship across contexts and disciplines. I write from the perspective of an anthropologist, however, whose discipline has long had trouble being truly interested in friendship. Part of the problem comes from relative perceptions of friendship’s universality: friendship has been seen as either not universal, too universal, or not universal(ly important) enough to merit much sustained attention. The works under consideration here show that even beyond anthropology, scholarship on friendship and other topics is always affected by questions of universalism. Specifically, these works indicate that relatively unreflective positions on universalist modes of description (including the reaction to them, what it means to seek particulars) can curtail understandings. This is not a blanket rejection of universalizing orientations. Rather, I argue that, instead of ignoring the problem of the universal—simply assuming that universalizing is not what particularists do—we need to understand how universalism appears in our scholarship, which means understanding what the limits of particularism are, too. Ultimately, if we can admit that elements of universalism always shadow how scholars think, we can then also concede that what some scholars have called generics can sometimes help us to be better, more measured particularists. To this end, I offer the generic of friendship’s mystic affordances, to improve our empirical

items.title: Ibn Khaldûn as a Colonial Archive: Toward an Epistemic Decolonization
items.source: Comparative Studies in Society and History

extra.summary: Abstract This article examines Ibn Khaldûn not as a stable, timeless precursor of modern social science but as a figure constituted through colonial translation and reception. Focusing on nineteenth- and twentieth-century French and English translations of the Muqaddimah , it argues that Ibn Khaldûn emerged in modern scholarship as a colonial archive—a site where translation, race, and epistemic authority intersected to produce new forms of historical and sociological knowledge. Through close comparison of Arabic originals and their European translations, the article shows how colonial epistemologies reconfigured Ibn Khaldûn’s analytical categories—particularly those concerning tribe, generation, civilization, and climate—into racialized frameworks foreign to his medieval context. It further demonstrates how this translated Ibn Khaldûn became selectively relevant to European social science while remaining excluded from its canonical genealogies. Finally, the article critically reassesses the enduring claim that Ibn Khaldûn articulated racist views about Black populations, showing that this attribution itself belongs to the colonial archive generated through translation rather than to the epistemic logic of the original text. The article thus contributes to comparative histories of knowledge, colonial epistemology, and the global formation of the social sciences.

items.title: Borrowed Time: Sovereign Debt and Temporal Disorder In Socialist Yugoslavia
items.source: Comparative Studies in Society and History

extra.summary: Abstract When Francis Fukuyama described the collapse of state socialism as marking the “end of history,” he captured the imagination of the post-Cold War moment, rendering the fall of the Berlin Wall a metonym for the definitive eclipse of communism and the advent of a new era of liberal capitalist hegemony. For Europe’s Left, the term became associated with a moment of profound demoralization. Fukuyama’s end of history, however, was only one moment of a longer and more expansive crisis in the socialist order of time. This crisis can be traced back to the global economic upheavals of the 1970s that impacted both social democracy in the West and state socialism in the East. A decade before crowds forced their way across a divided Berlin, socialism on both sides of the Iron Curtain had entered an existential decline. This article argues that the sovereign debt crises that beset European states in the final decade of the Cold War disrupted socialism’s regime of historicity. It develops this argument with reference to late-socialist Yugoslavia and demonstrates how the temporal conditions of sovereign indebtedness shaped popular culture. Through a reading of the films Balkanski špijun (1984) and Već viđeno (1987), the article argues that the erosion of socialism’s horizons of expectation fostered a new experience of historical time in which the past returned in uncanny, troubling, and ultimately destructive ways.

extra.summary: Abstract Via an examination of comparative approaches to radically violent societies such as Nazi Germany and colonial Australia, this article investigates how German representations of Australian state racism shed light on the similarities and differences between the Holocaust and frontier violence in Australia. Indicative of these German views, it suggests, were those of government officials like Rudolf Asmis, who frequently wrote and spoke on the question of radical violence against Indigenous people in Australia against the backdrop of increasing antisemitic violence in Germany that culminated in the Holocaust. Assessing the position of Australia in Nazi views on the racial state, it suggests that there are important differences between settler colonial violence and the Holocaust that can only be uncovered through comparative historical method.

items.title: Culture and Contradiction Before the End of History: From Socialist Legacies to Market Logics
items.source: Comparative Studies in Society and History

extra.summary: Abstract In late-socialist Romania, the state sought to govern economic crisis by demanding market-like conduct from cultural institutions while continuing to bind them to the political structures of socialism. Drawing on archival planning reports, media accounts, and post-socialist recollections, this article traces the emergence of a “self-financing regime” that reorganized cultural production around revenue generation, entrepreneurial conduct, and managerial accountability. I argue that self-financing constituted neither a retreat of socialism nor an incipient transition to capitalism, but an experiment in governing crisis by relocating the burdens of economic survival onto institutions themselves. This shift generated a contradictory institutional world: cultural actors were compelled to pursue economic self-sufficiency and become self-optimizing subjects even as markets remained ideologically repudiated, socialist obligations endured, and nominal decentralization extended bureaucratic oversight. Yet contradiction did not simply signal the incoherence of late socialism. As these tensions became embedded in everyday institutional practice, contradiction provided the very means through which austerity was rendered governable. The Romanian case thus shows how market-like rationalities could emerge from within socialist crisis management and crystallize into historically distinct forms of governance. The article engages with the concept of affective circuits (Cole, J., and C. Groes. 2016. Affective Circuits: African Migrations to Europe and the Pursuit of Social Regeneration. 1st ed., vol. 57734. The University of Chicago Press) to highlight how affective dimensions of care interweave with material elements, and to show how exerting material care is closely connected to social becoming. It further shows how essential care practices are displaced from the hands of young people and their families to frontline workers in the welfare state, which is argued to lead to what (Lynch, K. 2022. Care and Capitalism. Polity Press) has termed affective inequality. Through engagements with the sociological and anthropological scholarship on everyday care and relational justice, the article argues that the current migration regime in Denmark displaces refugees’ care practices to frontline workers and causes relational injustice.

items.title: The (He)art of doing research with undocumented migrants: a duoethnography on positionality, emotion and moral conflict
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
items.affiliation: Leiden University; University of Humanistic Studies

extra.summary: Building on the reflexive turn in migration studies, this article examines how ethnographic researchers negotiate moral conflict during and after fieldwork with undocumented migrants. As an important, yet often-overlooked, dimension of migration research, we conceptualise moral conflict as the tension between professional expectations, institutional constraints, and researchers’ own moral convictions. To explore and examine this issue, we adopt the innovative methodological approach of duoethnography, treating the authors’ dialogical encounters as the primary site of inquiry. Drawing on conversations about our experience conducting ethnographic research with undocumented migrants in the Netherlands and Belgium, we jointly analyse how moral conflict is negotiated across four interconnected domains: roles, care, knowledge, and change. Our findings show that moral conflict is not merely an individual emotional construct, but also a relational force shaping positionality, ethical decision-making, and knowledge production. Rather than treating emotions and vulnerability as threats to scholarly rigour, we argue that collaborative reflexivity can deepen ethical sensitivity and analytical insight. By introducing duoethnography to migration studies, this article offers both a conceptual vocabulary for researchers’ moral conflicts and a methodological framework for more reflexive, caring, and ethically engaged scholarship.

items.title: Lost passes: the quest of African footballers for a football career in Turkey
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: This article examines the migratory trajectories of African footballers in Turkey, asking how aspirations unfold within a football space imagined as a gateway to Europe but experienced as a site of prolonged waiting and blocked mobility. Drawing on multi-perspective qualitative fieldwork within the SiNAFE project (interviews with migrant footballers, coaches, agents, journalists, and community actors, and sustained ethnographic engagement with African migrant communities in Istanbul), the analysis reconstructs a narrative arc of football migration to Turkey in six stages, from the formation of aspiration in West Africa to a condition of suspension between football and survival labour. Unlike arcs ordered towards a stage of settlement, the arc reconstructed here rarely completes: players circulate between recalibration, precarious labour and waiting, unable to advance within Turkish football or move onward to Europe. This suspended arc makes visible the specificity of Turkey as a liminal migration space, neither destination nor functioning transit corridor, where legal suspension is compounded by a football wait that never resolves into arrival, and where informal, person-dependent football structures set the terms of play. It also sharpens the tension between football migration and labour migration, showing how footballers become workers who train, and how football's success stories obscure the migrant condition beneath them.

extra.summary: This article examines how Berlin's Kurdish diaspora and diaspora-centric Kurdistan's Jews in Jerusalem embrace music performances to meet their cultural, political, and social affairs. Based on ethnographic field research, including 87 in-depth interviews and participant observations, the article explores how individual singers, music bands, cultural associations, and religious institutions perform and facilitate music to impact diasporic life. items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: As motherhood extends from the private sphere to the public arena of social media, it can no longer be understood merely as a form of social division of labour. Instead, it becomes an identity position that requires continuous justification and maintenance. Drawing on digital ethnographic observation of 15 migrant mother bloggers, combined with a multimodal critical discourse analysis of their video content, this study examines how they continuously negotiate with the internally heterogeneous and at times contradictory gaze within the homeland public sphere, responding to, reconciling, and reinterpreting competing imaginaries and expectations of motherhood. In doing so, they develop an interconnected structure of legitimacy argumentation concerning the social recognizability of their migrant motherhood, organised around three dimensions: cognitive–professional, moral–subjective, and existential–livability. The study ultimately proposes ‘maternal legitimacy work’ as an analytical perspective, shifting the focus from the formation of migrant motherhood imaginaries toward a relational perspective on their production, thereby capturing how motherhood imaginaries are constructed under public scrutiny and justified as social positions that can be understood, accepted, and recognised.

items.title: Immigration for realists: how we misread the public and the evidence, and how to do better
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: Immigration experts have never known more, and rarely mattered less. Restrictionist parties and arguments have become increasingly influential across immigrant-receiving democracies, even as the expert consensus on immigration's benefits has grown more confident. I argue that we, immigration scholars and practitioners, have ourselves contributed to this gap. First, we misread the public: most voters are neither committed xenophobes nor dormant cosmopolitans. Rather, they are conditional supporters willing to accept immigration they see as beneficial to their country. Their underlying preferences are strikingly stable, with opponents usually caring more about the issue than supporters. Second, we misrepresent the evidence on immigration's costs and benefits through selective framing and strategic omission. While the effects of freer human mobility are generally positive, these findings come with qualifications that experts often leave out. Voters who notice a mismatch with their experience have good reason to distrust us, which damages the case for immigration regardless of what the populist far right does. I argue for an immigration realism that takes voters' preferences seriously and reports inconvenient evidence as readily as favourable evidence. Instead of trying to change opponents' minds, we should put more effort into designing demonstrably beneficial policy compromises that can retain majority support.

items.title: Ritual continuity amid architectural change: spatiality in Akha-Hani house-building ceremonies in Southwest China

extra.summary: This study examines the ritual space of Akha-Hani house-building ceremonies in Xishuangbanna, Southwest China. The analysis identifies three connected dimensions of ritual space: physical, social, and spiritual. Despite the shift from wooden to brick-concrete houses, key ritual nodes, including the central pillar, hearth, and Bahawuqu rooftop ornament, continue to link the household to ancestors and the wider cosmos. The article argues that ritual spatiality enables the Akha-Hani to reproduce kinship order and maintain cosmological boundaries amid architectural change. It further suggests that this tripartite model helps explain cultural continuity through material transformation.

items.title: Resettlement and spatial transformation: reconstructing sacred space in Wa homes in Yunnan, China

items.title: Bridging Policy and Practice: Implementing Culturally Responsive Pedagogy in an Ethnically Diverse Primary School in Yunnan, China

extra.summary: This study examines the policy–practice nexus in implementing Culturally Responsive Pedagogy (CRP) in an ethnically diverse primary school in Yunnan Province, China. Through policy document analysis, interviews with eight educators (including the principal), and 20 classroom observations, we identify systemic gaps between provincial CRP policies (e.g., bilingual mandates, cultural curriculum, teacher training) and their enactment. Key barriers include rigid curriculum scheduling, resource shortages (e.g., lack of bilingual materials and trained teachers), and decontextualized professional development. While policies rhetorically endorse CRP, classroom practices remain episodic and symbolic, failing to structurally integrate minority cultures. Nevertheless, teacher-initiated adaptations, such as glossing Chinese vocabulary in Wa and embedding cultural artifacts (e.g., Kongming lanterns) into science instruction, measurably raised student engagement, suggesting that even bounded, episodic responsiveness can yield instructional gains within structural constraints. Drawing on James A. Banks’ Transformation Approach, we argue for systemic reforms: flexible curriculum frameworks, targeted resource allocation, and community-embedded teacher training. The study underscores the need to shift from additive cultural inclusion to transformative pedagogical redesign to achieve equity in Yunnan’s ethnically diverse context.

This essay draws on critical infrastructure and hydrosocial theory to present river crossings as “hydrosocial mobility infrastructures” (HMIs) enabling connectivity within the wider system of historical trade routes linking China and Tibet in the headwaters region. The HMI framework highlights the ecological and relational character of pre-1950s river crossings, which are shaped by human and non-human interactions, local ecological knowledge, overlapping authorities, and frontier geopolitics, as well as by hydrological, geomorphic, and seasonal changes.

The study argues that current pension frameworks inadequately reflect the realities of many in the Chinese community, resulting in welfare exclusion. Social implications The findings underscore the need for pension frameworks and welfare
topics: Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues

items.title: Cooperative experimental governance in left-behind border regions: Digital transformation of imported fresh fruit distribution in Pingxiang city, China

extra.summary: Research on left-behind regions increasingly emphasizes place-based and neo-endogenous development, yet how digital platforms as extra-regional actors trigger and the subsequent regional transformation in left-behind border regions of emerging economies remains underexplored. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork conducted between 2023 and 2025, this paper examines the digital transformation of imported fresh fruit distribution in Pingxiang, a county-level city in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region of China along the border with Vietnam. It traces three phases of transformation of Pingxiang: platform-triggered grassroots adaptation, in which flexible border-trade arrangements enabled small traders to exploit digital platform-based market access; cooperative institutional experimentation, in which local authorities selectively incorporated extra-regional wholesale capabilities to stabilize distribution; and state-led infrastructural recentering, in which digital trade and distribution became increasingly organized through locally anchored, state-backed infrastructure under tighter border regulation. To explain these shifts, the paper develops cooperative experimental governance as a territorially embedded mode of governance through which state actors selectively coordinate with heterogeneous market actors to stabilize and redirect digital platform-triggered transformation in left-behind border regions. Digital platforms are thus understood as institutional triggers rather than stable
topics: Global trade, sustainability, and social impact

items.title: Beyond Resource Transfer: The Action Logic and Innovative Patterns of Counterpart Assistance for Rural Revitalization in Western China
items.affiliation: Guilin University of Technology; Beihang University

extra.summary: Regional inequality remains a persistent challenge for development governance. When external support is disconnected from local conditions or excessively displaces local actors, resource inputs may fail to generate sustainable development and even weaken local agency. To examine how external support can be transformed into sustainable local capacity, this study integrates neo-endogenous development theory with synergetics to develop an “exogenous–endogenous synergy” framework. Drawing on multiple rounds of fieldwork and interviews, the study finds that Guangdong–Guangxi collaboration has shifted from compensatory resource transfer towards capacity building and institutional embedding. This transformation operates through three interrelated mechanisms: coordinated guidance, multidimensional incentives, and digital empowerment. Variations in local resource endowments and ideational capacity give rise to three context-contingent pathways: integrated advancement, ideational activation, and resource mobilization, each representing a pathway towards an ideal-type model. The findings suggest that cross-regional collaboration may reduce regional inequality when transferred resources are converted into sustainable local capacity, thereby strengthening rather than substituting for local agency.

items.title: How Technological Innovation Shapes the Digital Transformation-Performance Link: Engagement and Well-Being Pathways in Chinese State-Owned Enterprises

extra.summary: Digital transformation may offer employees useful work resources while introducing additional demands. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, this study examines individual-level associations between perceived digital transformation and employee performance, with employee engagement and psychological well-being as parallel statistical mediators and perceived technological innovation as a moderator. Cross-sectional survey data were obtained from 500 employees in 58 state-owned enterprises in Guangxi, China. Regression analyses with HC3 robust standard errors and bootstrap confidence intervals indicated a positive bivariate association between perceived digital transformation and employee performance. Positive conditional indirect associations were observed through both employee engagement and psychological well-being. Perceived technological innovation positively moderated the conditional direct association and both first-stage associations, although the incremental interaction magnitudes were small. Johnson–Neyman analysis suggested a negative conditional direct association in the very low moderator region, containing 51 respondents (10.2%), and a positive association in the upper region, containing 321 respondents (64.2%). These sample-specific findings warrant cautious interpretation, particularly in the sparsely represented lower region. items.title: Synergistic Evolution of Ecological Product Value Realization and Sustainable Rural Development: A Grounded Theory Study of the Liubao Tea Industry in China

extra.summary: Different from conventional ecosystem services valuation, which mainly focuses on identifying and measuring ecological values, EPVR emphasizes the institutional and industrial processes through which ecological values are transformed into economic and social benefits. Exploring the relationship between ecological product value realization and rural revitalization is crucial for addressing the insufficient transformation of ecological advantages into rural development momentum and the limited reciprocal contribution of specialty industries to local society. Taking the Liubao tea industry in Wuzhou, Guangxi, as a case, this study uses a grounded theory approach informed by a synergistic evolution perspective to examine the changing condition–action–outcome configurations between ecological product value realization and rural revitalization during industrial development. The findings show that ecological product value realization follows a phased trajectory from ecological resource value to ecological industry value and then to ecological asset value, while rural revitalization evolves from poverty alleviation-driven revitalization to the deepening of industrial revitalization and finally to agglomeration for fusion-driven revitalization. Across these trajectories, the synergistic relationship takes three dominant forms—resource mutual promotion, industrial interaction, and fusion synergy. The staged pattern reflects changes in both ecological value forms and rural participation

items.title: Understanding Organisational Culture: A Review of Definitions, Theoretical Frameworks, and Empirical Studies
items.source: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences

extra.summary: Organisational culture is widely recognised as a key factor influencing organisational effectiveness, employee behaviour, and institutional development. This paper reviews the major definitions, theoretical foundations, and empirical studies related to organisational culture. It first examines influential perspectives proposed by Schein (1985, 2010), Hofstede (1991), Cameron and Quinn (1999), Denison (1990), and Ouchi (1981), highlighting the evolution of the concept from shared assumptions and values to multidimensional and performance-oriented frameworks. The paper then discusses Harrison and Stokes’s (1992) Organisational Culture Theory and its alignment with the five dimensions of the Organisational Culture Scale developed by Huang and Teo (2019): Goal Orientation, Participative Decision Making, Formal Relationships, Innovation Orientation, and Shared Vision. In addition, empirical studies conducted in international higher education settings, across China, and specifically in Inner Mongolia are reviewed to identify major research trends and gaps. The review indicates that although organisational culture has been extensively studied, limited attention has been paid to ethnic minority regions, multi-level cultural influences, and the mechanisms through which culture affects important psychological and organisational outcomes. items.title: More-than-human community in “naked” cider making: An autoethnography in the RBLD cidery
items.source: International Journal of Gastronomy and Food Science

extra.summary: The artisanal production of fermented beverages constitutes a particularly fertile ground for exploring human-nonhuman relationships in contemporary food systems. This article analyzes the RBLD project, an initiative producing "naked" ciders developed in a family orchard in the Basque Country between 2019 and 2026. Drawing on an anthropological approach that combines analytical autoethnography, sensory ethnography, and multispecies ethnography, this study examines the relationships connecting apple trees, microorganisms, pollinating insects, animals, materials, climatic conditions, and humans in the cider-making process. The results show that cider emerges from a more-than-human community whose participation spans all stages of the process, from flowering and harvest to fermentation and tasting. Prolonged engagement in these relationships progressively transformed the cider maker's modes of attention and knowledge, while shaping the production practices developed within the RBLD project. Consequently, cider production began to be understood less as an activity aimed at technical control and more as a practice of respect toward this community. This article proposes understanding cider as a material and temporal condensation of a more-than-human community and suggests that so-called "naked" ciders offer a way to allow this community to continue expressing itself through the beverage. items.title: Missiological engagement with anthropology in the early 20th century

extra.summary: Anthropology has been a critical dialogue partner for missiology since the inception of both fields of inquiry. Despite this, many missiologists are unaware of the important forays into anthropological theory and practice that missionaries made in the early 20th century. This article reviews and analyzes the contributions of missionaries and anthropologists, especially those that were made in the premier missiological journal of that period, the International Review of Missions. As the field of missiology in North America engages with questions about its future role in academic discourse as well as in practical missionary training, learning from our discipline’s past engagement with anthropology is critical.

items.title: Mobilizing theory in mathematics teaching: a praxeological analysis of the theory-practice problem in teachers’ instructional justifications

extra.summary: While educational theories are emphasized in pre-service teacher education, questions remain about how such knowledge is expressed in classroom practice. Previous research shows that teachers do not always make theoretical justification explicit and that instructional decisions are often shaped by classroom experience. This study examines this issue through praxeological analysis based on the Anthropological Theory of the Didactic, which distinguishes between the practical block (tasks and techniques) and the logos block (technology and theory). A multiple-case study was conducted with six secondary mathematics teachers. The analysis examined teachers’ instructional justifications during observed lessons. The findings show that teachers consistently justified their instructional strategies, but these justifications were expressed mainly in terms of classroom workability. Technological justification was also evident, particularly in lessons requiring comparison and conceptual distinction, though it varied across cases. Explicit theoretical justification was limited and appeared only in selected lesson episodes. These findings suggest that mobilizing theory in practice does not necessarily require explicit theoretical discourse. Instead, teachers’ instructional justifications are often local and context-sensitive. The study highlights the value of praxeology for examining how teachers express instructional justifications and how theory is mobilized in classroom practice.

items.title: Instructional design of majāz in Arabic textbooks: a praxeological review for non-native secondary learners
items.affiliation: Indonesia University of Education; National University of Malaysia

extra.summary: Purpose This study aims to propose a structured didactic design for teaching majāz (figurative language) to non-native Arabic secondary learners by utilizing Chevallard’s Anthropological Theory of the Didactic. It specifically addresses the “didactic gap” between complex rhetorical tasks and the cognitive scaffolding provided in learning materials. Design/methodology/approach The study employs a qualitative, interpretive document analysis of a purposive corpus of Arabic textbooks designed for non-native secondary learners. Using a theory-driven praxeological framework (T, τ, θ, Θ). The analytical focus is placed on the didactic transposition of majāz concepts. To ensure validity and trustworthiness, the study utilizes theoretical and analyst triangulation. Findings The analysis uncovers a critical praxeological misalignment: highly demanding identification tasks (T) are presented without explicit cognitive techniques (τ), relying instead on abstract classical definitions (θ). To bridge this gap, this study proposes a reformed instructional design featuring a “Three-Step Semantic Decoding Algorithm” (detecting semantic anomalies, mapping conceptual domains, and reconstructing figurative meaning). Research limitations/implications Practically, the findings offer an operational guide for curriculum developers and textbook authors to design scaffolded rhetorical tasks and visual aids.
